summary: The Maldives grants a free 30-day tourist visa on arrival to every nationality — one of the only truly universal visa-on-arrival policies in the world — provided you have a confirmed hotel booking, sufficient funds and an onward ticket. Every traveler must also submit the free Imuga Traveller Declaration online within 96 hours before arrival, and the stay can be extended in-country to a total of 90 days.

fee.notes: Free of charge for every nationality. Granted at the border for up to 30 days, subject to a confirmed accommodation booking, sufficient funds and an onward or return ticket.

visaTypes.name: Tourist Visa Extension (up to 90 days total)

fee.notes: Apply through the Imuga portal before your initial 30 days expire; the fee and process are set by Maldives Immigration and can change. Confirm before applying. Continued proof of accommodation and funds is required.

passportValidity.text: Your passport (or travel document) must be machine-readable and valid for at least 1 month on arrival — though at least 6 months is recommended, as some airlines apply the stricter standard.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate (ICVP) is required only if you arrive from, or transited through, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission.

travelInsurance.text: Not an entry requirement, but strongly recommended — serious medical cases often require evacuation by seaplane or flight to Malé or abroad, which is extremely expensive without cover.

onwardTicket.text: A confirmed onward or return ticket is one of the conditions of the visa on arrival — airlines and immigration officers check it.

proofOfFunds.text: You must show means to cover your stay; the commonly applied benchmark is about USD 100 plus USD 50 per day, waived in practice when you hold a confirmed booking at a registered tourist facility.

declarations.name: Imuga Traveller Declaration
declarations.submitWindow: Within 96 hours before arrival (and again before departure)
declarations.text: All travelers must submit the free Imuga Traveller Declaration online within 96 hours before both arrival and departure. Keep the QR code on your phone or printed. It is checked at check-in and at the border.

notes: Importing alcohol is strictly prohibited — bottles (including duty-free bought abroad) are held at the airport and returned on departure.
Pork products, religious idols for worship and pornographic material are also prohibited imports.
Drones must be declared; flying them near resorts or Malé requires permission.

payments.text: Resorts and liveaboards take cards and bill in US dollars, which are accepted almost everywhere alongside rufiyaa. On local islands carry some cash (small USD bills or MVR); a 10% service charge plus 16% TGST is added to most resort bills.

safety.text: The Maldives is a safe destination, especially on resort islands. Petty theft can occur in Malé and on local islands; the biggest real risks are strong ocean currents and snorkelling or diving incidents — follow local guidance.

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to April is the dry northeast-monsoon season — sunny skies, calm seas and the best visibility for diving. May to October is wetter and windier but cheaper.

idp.text: Maldives is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Maldives is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Maldives yet.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

tips.text: Alcohol is legal only on resort islands and liveaboards. It is illegal to import it (even duty-free) or to drink on local inhabited islands, including Malé.

On local inhabited islands dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered) and swim only at designated "bikini beaches"; during Ramadan, eat and drink discreetly in public. Resort islands have no such restrictions.

The Imuga Traveller Declaration is free at imuga.immigration.gov.mv and must be submitted within 96 hours before your flight — for both arrival and departure. Ignore third-party sites that charge for it.
Tap water is not drinkable — resorts provide desalinated or bottled water. If you travel with a drone, declare it on arrival; many resorts and Malé airspace restrict flying.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for the Maldives?
faq.answer: No advance visa, whatever your passport. Every nationality receives a free 30-day tourist visa on arrival, provided you have a confirmed accommodation booking, means to cover your stay, an onward or return ticket and a submitted Imuga declaration.

faq.question: What is the Imuga Traveller Declaration?
faq.answer: Imuga is the Maldives' online traveler declaration, mandatory for all arrivals and departures. Submit it free at imuga.immigration.gov.mv within 96 hours before each flight and keep the QR code ready for check-in and immigration.

faq.question: Can I stay in the Maldives longer than 30 days?
faq.answer: Yes. The free 30-day visa on arrival can be extended in-country up to a total of 90 days by applying through Maldives Immigration (via the Imuga portal) before your first 30 days expire, with proof of accommodation and funds. A fee applies.

faq.question: Can I bring alcohol into the Maldives?
faq.answer: No. Importing alcohol is prohibited even in duty-free bags. It will be stored at the airport and returned when you leave. Alcohol is served legally only on resort islands and liveaboard boats, not on local inhabited islands.

faq.question: Do I need to change money into rufiyaa?
faq.answer: Usually not. US dollars are accepted almost everywhere and resorts bill in USD with cards widely accepted. Rufiyaa (MVR) is handy for small purchases on local islands. Bring small-denomination USD bills if you plan to leave the resort.
